items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: Louis had made the Saints, not really popular, but he'd made this record in 1937 or 1938

ctx.x: Yes. Right at the end of the line. You go to the end of the line and this place, the One Cent Club, it means that you buy one drink at the regular price and you get a second drink for one cent. It was during the Depression, of course. They had on big blue silk blouses with big long full sleeves, you know, sort of like clowns wear. Not that they were trying to make clowns out of them, but I mean, it was a special uniform they wore. A drummer, I believe it must have been, I'm not sure, unless I, until I look up my…
I heard that song as a white religious piece.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: so I went backstage and got to talk to him quite a while

ctx.x: Let me move this mic a little closer to you. Your voice is soft.

Was Louis Armstrong in New York at this time playing with... Well he was traveling all around. I actually interviewed him for the book up at the, I think it was up above the Apollo Theater or someplace in that block where they were having a rehearsal. I see. And then poor Louis wanted to play the Cavalieria Rusticana. What do they call it?

intermezzo comes between acts or something there in the opera just a slow number in 3-4 time it isn't a waltz or anything just a slower thing than that and he had a very nice arrangement that he was doing and playing the melody more or less straight and Joe Glazer had an assistant there, Joe Glazer was still his manager, was already his manager had been for years I guess even then so finally his manager told him he couldn't use that number gee Louie was so mad he said someday I'm going up there and tell those so…

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1975-02-02
items.q: Well, as Louis told me once, he blamed it onto the horses or something like that

ctx.x: So anyway, to get back to the point, Gene Williams had heard these records and agreed with me too that at least Bunk showed some possibilities. You couldn't really tell much how he played, both because his lip wasn't in shape and just by himself. The type of trumpet playing that Bunk did, which was a remarkable thing, and yet by itself it wouldn't sound that effective. Bunk was hardly ever on the beat, so if you didn't hear him patting his foot and all there, you could really tell of course where the beat is, but…
Well, of course, we'll never know what Joe Oliver really sounded like.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-08-31
items.q: Before that I'd gone to see people like Jimmy Noon, Johnny Dodds, and Armstrong, and met a few of my favorite New Orleans musicians.

ctx.x: You want to talk about some of these musicians you've encountered in the course of your career now?

Yes, I might talk a little bit. I happened to pick up an old big box at home I have called Notes, and I dug out a few of the notebooks and other things. One package of notes envelope called Jazzmen material that we collected in 1938 when we were working on Jazzmen. Unfortunately then, we not only didn't have tape recording, we didn't have any other recorders. Nobody was hardly recording interviews. When I started out about that time, they were using mostly aluminum blanks there for a while. You had to play with…
